paragraphs: The paper introduces a clustering algorithm that compresses data while preserving information about supplied categories. Its objective uses mutual information, which measures how much knowing one variable tells us about another. This gives clustering a specific purpose: groups should retain distinctions that help identify the categories, even as the representation becomes smaller.

The algorithm builds clusters from the bottom up and uses hard assignments, meaning that an item belongs to a single cluster. The authors connect this approach to the information bottleneck method, comparing it with a version that works from the top down and allows soft assignments. They establish a relationship between the results of these two approaches.

The method is demonstrated on the 20 Newsgroups dataset. For a subset containing two newsgroups, the authors report roughly a thousandfold compression while losing only 10% of the original mutual information. That result illustrates substantial preservation of category information under compression in the stated example; it does not describe performance across every clustering problem.
neurips-1999-agglomerative-information-b.tldr: A bottom-up clustering algorithm achieves substantial compression while preserving most category information in a two-newsgroup example.

paragraphs: The paper presents a neural model for separating speech from interfering sounds. The central problem is deciding which parts of a mixed acoustic input belong to the same sound stream. Its approach uses the timing relationships among neural oscillators as a way to represent those groupings.

The model contains a two-layer network of oscillators. Oscillators representing one stream synchronize with one another, while populations representing different streams remain out of synchrony. In this representation, coordinated activity identifies elements as belonging together. Differences in coordination allow separate streams to coexist in the network without being represented as a single combined source.

The authors evaluate the model on a corpus containing speech mixed with interfering sounds. They report an improvement in signal-to-noise ratio for every mixture tested, indicating that speech becomes stronger relative to interference according to that measure. The finding supports oscillatory correlation as a useful grouping mechanism for the evaluated mixtures, with synchronized populations providing the link between the neural representation and sound separation.
neurips-1999-an-oscillatory-correlation-.tldr: A neural oscillator network groups sound streams through synchrony and improves signal-to-noise ratio for every tested speech mixture.

paragraphs: The paper explores how matching timing across sound and vision can help a computer locate a sound source. Its motivation comes from the ventriloquism effect: synchronized visual events can influence where people perceive a sound to originate. An actor's visible mouth movements, for example, can make television audio seem to come from the actor.

The authors develop a system that searches a visual scene for regions whose activity correlates strongly with the acoustic signal. Those regions are marked as likely locations of a sound source. The underlying idea is that a visible event and a sound occurring together provide evidence of a shared source, making audiovisual timing useful for localization.

The paper discusses implementation experience and presents results on locating a speaker. It also considers possible applications of the approach. The contribution is a concrete way to use synchronization as a localization cue: the system produces candidate source regions from relationships between the two signals, preserving the distinction between a likely source and a conclusively identified one.
neurips-1999-audio-vision-using-audio-vi.tldr: A system locates likely sound sources by finding visual regions whose activity synchronizes with the audio.

paragraphs: The paper develops a silicon neuron implemented as a VLSI circuit and a corresponding mathematical description. The mathematical model uses two state variables to describe the system's changing condition. Having both a physical circuit and a compact model lets the authors compare measured behavior with behavior predicted through mathematical analysis.

The analysis focuses on what happens as the externally applied current changes. Using bifurcation analysis, the authors examine how changes in this control parameter alter the model's qualitative behavior. This addresses how the system's dynamics depend on its input current, extending the comparison beyond observing the circuit under one fixed operating condition.

The silicon neuron is examined under conditions corresponding to those used in the analysis. Its observed behavior agrees well with the mathematical predictions. This agreement supports the model as a description of the circuit under those conditions and shows the value of studying the hardware and its equations together: mathematical changes in behavior can be checked against a physical implementation.
neurips-1999-bifurcation-analysis-of-a-s.tldr: A two-state mathematical model predicts changes in a silicon neuron's behavior as applied current varies.

paragraphs: The paper extends the theoretical connection between decision-tree learning and boosting to trees with more than two branches at a split. Existing boosting results covered binary branching, but allowing additional branches changes the trade-off involved in growing a tree. A split can improve the tree's quality while also making its structure more elaborate.

Practical algorithms such as CART and C4.5 already balance the number of branches against improvement measured by a tree-quality index. The authors provide a boosting justification for a particular mathematical form of that balance. The required improvement grows in proportion to the logarithm of the number of branches.

The main theorem states, in essence, that top-down greedy tree construction remains an effective boosting algorithm when this improvement requirement is met. This is a conditional guarantee: the quality gain must satisfy the stated relationship to branching. Its significance is to give a theoretical basis for evaluating multi-way splits, connecting a local choice during tree construction to the broader boosting interpretation.
neurips-1999-boosting-with-multi-way-bra.tldr: Multi-way decision-tree growth retains a boosting guarantee when split improvement scales with the logarithm of the branch count.

paragraphs: The paper studies how a mobile robot can plan a route that leaves it with little uncertainty about its position when it reaches its goal. This matters because reliable localization cannot always be assumed. A route must therefore be evaluated partly by how uncertain the robot's position may become along the way.

The proposed method makes positional uncertainty an explicit part of the planning state. It generates trajectories through a space containing both the robot's pose and its uncertainty. This allows the planner to seek routes that minimize uncertainty at the destination. The motivation includes the computational difficulty of using partially observable Markov decision processes for large state spaces.

Experiments show that coastal navigation reduces uncertainty at the goal, especially when localization is degraded. The result supports accounting for localization quality during route planning. By seeking a destination state with lower positional uncertainty, the method reduces the likelihood of the robot becoming lost, making confidence about arrival part of the planning objective.
neurips-1999-coastal-navigation-with-mob.tldr: Planning jointly over robot pose and positional uncertainty reduces uncertainty at the goal, especially with degraded localization.

paragraphs: The paper addresses models whose desired behavior depends on how their outputs respond to changes in their inputs. This local response is described by the Jacobian, a matrix containing the partial derivatives of outputs with respect to inputs. Specifying the desired input-output relationship can therefore also involve specifying properties of this matrix.

The authors introduce J-prop, an efficient method for computing exact derivatives of various simple functions of the Jacobian with respect to model parameters. There are two derivative relationships involved: the Jacobian describes sensitivity to inputs, and J-prop determines how a chosen measure of that sensitivity changes when the model's parameters change.

These parameter derivatives supply the information needed to adjust a model according to an objective involving its Jacobian. The method applies to any parameterized feedforward model, including nonlinear regression models, multilayer perceptrons, and radial basis function networks. Its contribution is a general computational procedure for this class of derivative calculations, allowing input sensitivity to be treated directly as a property to optimize.
neurips-1999-differentiating-functions-o.tldr: J-prop efficiently computes exact parameter derivatives for a variety of simple functions of a feedforward model's Jacobian.

paragraphs: The paper studies how supervised learning unfolds in layered neural networks when the available training data must be reused. Repeated exposure to a restricted dataset makes the evolution of learning important: fitting the examples already seen and performing well beyond those examples are distinct outcomes that can change differently during training.

The authors extend an existing mathematical framework to include noisy teachers, meaning that the source of supervision contains noise. Their theory predicts how both training error and generalization error develop over time. Tracking both quantities makes it possible to describe the learning process in terms of its changing fit to training data and its changing ability to generalize.

The stated contribution is an expansion of the learning processes that can be solved mathematically for large neural networks. The extended framework includes situations in which overfitting can occur, and the authors describe its predictions as reliable. This makes the theory relevant to the combination of reused data and noisy supervision, where training progress alone does not fully describe learning quality.
neurips-1999-dynamics-of-supervised-lear.tldr: An extended theory predicts training and generalization dynamics for large networks learning from reused data and noisy teachers.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how a neural network can learn spatial relationships from the order in which it encounters objects. Spatial clues can come directly from position information, such as where something falls on the retina, or indirectly from timing. The indirect clue depends on a general tendency: objects encountered close together in time are often close together in space.

The researchers train networks on a prediction task involving objects arranged in a spatial layout. When training supplies temporal sequences without direct position information, the networks develop internal representations whose distances correlate with distances in that layout. This finding suggests that sequential experience can convey spatial structure. The reported correlation does not establish that the learned representation reproduces the layout exactly.

To examine the contribution of direct spatial cues, the researchers also supply position information during training that either agrees or conflicts with the layout. This setup lets them investigate the relative contributions of explicit spatial information and temporal proximity. The central reported finding is that temporal sequences alone can support learning representations that reflect spatial distances.
neurips-1999-effects-of-spatial-and-temp.tldr: Networks trained on temporal sequences without direct spatial cues develop internal distances that correlate with distances between objects in the external layout.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm for sampling complex probability distributions. Such sampling explores a space of possible states and provides a way to work with distributions that are difficult to handle directly. Here, the motivating application is Bayesian learning in neural networks, where learning involves a distribution over possible model settings.

The algorithm generalizes the stochastic dynamics method by using the state space's intrinsic geometric structure during exploration. Geometry becomes part of how the sampler moves through the space. The stated purpose is to facilitate efficient sampling of complex distributions, making the structure of the problem useful in choosing how exploration proceeds.

Applied to Bayesian neural-network learning, the method was found to perform at least as well as the strongest comparison method described in the abstract while taking considerably less time. This is an empirical result for the reported application. Its significance is the combination of maintained sampling-related performance and reduced computation, supporting geometry-aware exploration as a promising approach in this setting.
neurips-1999-manifold-stochastic-dynamic.tldr: A geometry-aware MCMC method matched or exceeded the strongest reported comparison while taking substantially less time in Bayesian neural-network learning.

paragraphs: The paper quantifies how nonlinear processing within a neuron's dendrites can increase memory capacity. It compares two models: one adds inputs across the whole cell before applying a single threshold, while the other applies a threshold within each dendritic branch and then adds the branch outputs. This isolates the effect of where nonlinear processing occurs.

The analysis assumes binary-valued synaptic weights and estimates capacity by counting distinct input-output functions available to each model. Applying a fixed nonlinearity within each dendritic compartment substantially increases flexibility. For a realistically sized neuron, the nonlinear model's capacity can exceed that of a similarly sized linear model by more than a factor of ten.

The largest predicted gains occur with relatively many small dendritic subunits. The authors also train both models on randomized two-class classification problems using a stochastic delta rule. Large gains predicted by the analysis are achieved empirically, linking the function-counting argument to learned memory performance within the studied models.
neurips-1999-memory-capacity-of-linear-v.tldr: Under binary synaptic weights, branch-level nonlinearities can increase neuronal memory capacity more than tenfold, with predicted gains achieved experimentally.

paragraphs: The paper addresses parameter selection for support vector machines. Choosing parameter values determines which particular model is used, so the selection problem concerns judging alternatives rather than merely obtaining a solution for one fixed setting. The authors introduce mathematical scoring criteria, called functionals, intended to guide that judgment.

These criteria are based on the span of support vectors and on rescaling the feature space. Both connect model selection to the geometry of the representation used by the support vector machine. The proposed functionals turn those geometric concepts into quantities that can be used to assess parameter choices and compare their expected quality.

The authors show that the functionals can predict both the best parameter choice and the relative performance quality associated with any parameter value. These are related but distinct uses: identifying a preferred setting and assessing how other settings compare. The contribution is therefore a basis for evaluating the parameter landscape, providing model-selection information beyond a recommendation of one setting.
neurips-1999-model-selection-for-support.tldr: Geometric criteria based on support vectors and feature-space rescaling predict preferred SVM parameters and relative performance across settings.

paragraphs: Model predictive control chooses control actions by optimizing predicted process behavior over a future horizon. Its usefulness depends on the model used for those predictions. The paper addresses a common mismatch: industrial processes can be nonlinear, while their controllers often use linear models because nonlinear modeling and optimization can be difficult or computationally expensive.

The authors present a general neural-network technique for learning nonlinear dynamic process models from empirical data. They also show that these models can be used efficiently within model predictive control. The approach therefore addresses both constructing a nonlinear model and incorporating it into the optimization that selects control actions.

The paper reports successful industrial implementations in refining, petrochemicals, paper production, and food processing. It presents controller performance for a polyethylene reactor as a specific nonlinear industrial application. These implementations support the practical feasibility of the approach: learned nonlinear dynamics can participate in predictive control, connecting modeling from observed data with decisions about how an industrial process should be operated.
neurips-1999-neural-network-based-model-.tldr: Neural networks learn nonlinear process models that can be used efficiently in model predictive control, with successful industrial implementations.

paragraphs: The paper examines how accurately a population of neurons can encode stimuli with multiple dimensions when the neurons spike stochastically. It focuses on tuning widths, which describe how broadly a neuron responds across stimuli. The question is how the distribution of these widths across a population affects the information carried by its activity.

A commonly studied arrangement gives every neuron an identical, radially symmetric receptive field. The authors find this uniform arrangement disadvantageous from an information-theoretic perspective. Their comparison makes the organization of the population central: encoding accuracy depends on how response properties are distributed among neurons, including whether those properties are all alike.

Two changes improve encoding accuracy in the study: allowing tuning widths to vary and dividing the population into specialized subpopulations. The results identify diversity and specialization as useful features of the analyzed neural representation. They suggest that evaluating a population only through identical receptive fields can overlook encoding benefits available when neurons have different widths or take on specialized representational roles.
neurips-1999-neural-representation-of-mu.tldr: Variable tuning widths and specialized subpopulations improve encoding accuracy in the studied populations of stochastically spiking neurons.

paragraphs: The paper generalizes linear discriminant analysis to handle nonlinear class separation. Classical LDA finds a lower-dimensional representation in which class centers are spread apart and uses linear decision boundaries. This can be inadequate when the arrangement of the data requires more flexible boundaries to separate the classes.

The proposed approach uses kernel functions in place of dot products. This kernel formulation allows discriminant analysis to operate in a feature space and supports a nonlinear generalization of the original method. The central change is in the representation and its associated computations, extending the kinds of class structure that discriminant analysis can address.

The authors also formulate the expectation-maximization algorithm in terms of kernel functions. This provides a common framework for unsupervised mixture analysis, supervised discriminant analysis, and semi-supervised analysis with some observations left unlabeled. The contribution therefore joins nonlinear representation with different levels of label availability, allowing these learning settings to be expressed through a shared feature-space approach.
neurips-1999-nonlinear-discriminant-anal.tldr: Kernel-based discriminant analysis extends linear class separation and unifies supervised, unsupervised, and partially labeled learning through an EM formulation.

paragraphs: The paper treats input selection for a classifier resembling a radial basis function model as a Bayesian inference problem. The goal involves deciding which inputs to use while also estimating the model's coefficients. Both choices are represented through a posterior distribution, so uncertainty about the input subset becomes part of the learning problem.

The authors approximate this joint posterior using samples generated by Gibbs updates and reversible jump moves. Together, these operations explore model coefficients and alternative input subsets. Sampling supports an assessment of multiple candidate subsets and their posterior probabilities, linking the selection of inputs to uncertainty about the fitted model.

The method is evaluated on public datasets, with classification accuracy compared against a conventional automatic relevance determination scheme. The same datasets are used to infer posterior probabilities for different input subsets. The contribution thus includes both predictive evaluation and probabilistic input assessment: it examines classification performance while also estimating how strongly the data support particular choices of inputs.
neurips-1999-on-input-selection-with-rev.tldr: Bayesian sampling jointly estimates classifier coefficients and input subsets, yielding posterior probabilities for alternative feature selections.

paragraphs: The paper studies local linear regression, which makes predictions by fitting linear relationships in a neighborhood of interest. A weighting kernel determines how observations contribute to that local fit. Although the method often works well for low-dimensional forecasting, its performance typically deteriorates as the number of dimensions increases.

The authors investigate changing the shape of the weighting kernel as a possible response to this difficulty. Kernel shape governs how the local neighborhood is weighted across the input space. They propose a data-driven method for estimating an optimal shape, allowing this aspect of the regression procedure to be chosen using the observed data.

Experiments use both an artificially generated dataset and data from the UC Irvine repository. The reported results show benefits from kernel shaping. This supports adapting neighborhood geometry as a useful component of local linear regression in the tested settings. The approach addresses an aspect of the high-dimensional problem through weighting, without establishing that kernel shaping eliminates the curse of dimensionality.
neurips-1999-optimal-kernel-shapes-for-l.tldr: A data-driven method adapts weighting-kernel shape and shows benefits for local linear regression on synthetic and repository data.

paragraphs: The paper explores a possible computational role for the extensive recurrent excitation in neocortical circuits: predicting the next input from recent experience. Its starting point is physiological evidence that changes in recurrent synapses depend asymmetrically on event timing. The authors ask how this timing-dependent learning could support prediction of familiar input sequences.

They show that a temporal-difference learning rule for prediction, combined with action potentials that propagate back into dendrites, reproduces the observed temporally asymmetric Hebbian plasticity. This connects a learning objective with a physiological learning pattern. Recurrent connections could thereby be modified so that recent inputs help anticipate what is likely to arrive next.

Biophysical simulations show a cortical network learning to predict moving stimuli and developing direction-selective responses through learning. Model neurons also exhibit space-time response properties similar to those of direction-selective cells in alert monkey visual cortex. These findings support the proposed predictive role of recurrent circuitry through a combination of learning-rule correspondence and simulated response properties.
neurips-1999-predictive-sequence-learnin.tldr: A predictive learning mechanism reproduces timing-dependent cortical plasticity and produces direction-selective responses in biophysical simulations.

paragraphs: The paper makes nonlinear regression more robust by replacing a Gaussian noise model with a Student-t distribution. Its degrees-of-freedom parameter controls the distribution's form, connecting Gaussian behavior with the Cauchy distribution used in robust regression. This flexibility lets the noise model adapt to data containing unusually large errors.

The authors use the interpretation of the t-distribution as an infinite mixture of Gaussians to develop EM-based learning. Model parameters and hyperparameters, including degrees of freedom, can be estimated from data. By adapting this parameter, the system can effectively distinguish outliers from other observations and reduce inappropriate responses to extreme measurements.

Experiments on real-world datasets show improved predictors, particularly when outliers are present. The paper also examines online learning, where an unusual measurement can otherwise trigger an unsuitable weight update. In the reported experiments, the t-based noise model supports stable online learning and outperforms methods including the extended Kalman filter. These findings link the noise assumption directly to prediction quality and the stability of ongoing adaptation.
neurips-1999-robust-neural-network-regre.tldr: Learning a Student-t noise model improves regression robustness and produces stable online learning in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: The paper investigates where different kinds of information are located within speech across time and frequency. It distinguishes information about phonetic labels from information about the speaker or channel. This matters because a speech feature can be informative for one recognition task without having the same role in another.

The authors estimate mutual information between phonetic labels and individual features, along with joint mutual information for groups of two or three features. These calculations examine information available from features separately and together. They also extend Miller's bias formulas for entropy and mutual-information estimates with higher-order terms, addressing the estimation procedure used in the analysis.

Corresponding information estimates are made for speaker and channel recognition. The findings describe complementary spatial distributions within the time-frequency representation: phonetic information is spread locally, while speaker/channel information is spread globally. The result provides a task-dependent picture of informative speech components, showing why the scale over which features are considered matters when characterizing what a speech signal reveals.
neurips-1999-search-for-information-bear.tldr: Information estimates reveal local spreading of phonetic information and global spreading of speaker/channel information across speech time and frequency.

paragraphs: The paper studies initialization for speech models fitted with expectation-maximization. Speech is represented as a linear stochastic state-space system whose properties are stationary within successive segments. Poor initialization can produce poor formant trajectories, which track speech resonances important for vowel intelligibility. The authors investigate subspace identification as a better starting procedure.

They compare subspace state-space system identification, called 4SID, with EM. Both estimate a hidden state sequence and then model parameters, but they use different tools: Kalman filtering and least squares for 4SID, versus Kalman smoothing and maximum likelihood for EM. Their structural similarity motivates using 4SID to initialize EM.

4SID requires neither iteration nor initialization, although it is probabilistically suboptimal compared with EM. Experiments on real speech find that the subspace methods compare favorably with conventional initialization techniques, producing smoother formant trajectories, greater frequency resolution, and higher likelihoods. The approach uses a convenient initial estimator to support an iterative probabilistic method, with improvements reported in quantities directly relevant to speech modeling.
neurips-1999-speech-modelling-using-subs.tldr: Subspace identification provides effective initialization for EM speech modeling, improving formant trajectories, frequency resolution, and likelihoods in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper examines when a learning rule defined by individual spike times can be approximated using firing rates. These descriptions operate at different levels: one depends on the ordering of discrete neural events, while the other summarizes activity through rates. Connecting them helps explain how a spike-level mechanism can influence network dynamics.

The authors consider differential anti-Hebbian plasticity. In this rule, a synapse weakens when a presynaptic spike precedes a postsynaptic spike and strengthens when that order is reversed. Under certain conditions, the timing-based rule can be approximated by a rule depending on the time derivative of the postsynaptic firing rate, meaning how quickly that rate changes.

The resulting rate-based rule acts to stabilize persistent activity patterns in recurrent neural networks. This links sensitivity to temporal ordering at individual synapses with stability at the network level. The approximation is explicitly conditional, so the connection depends on the circumstances under which spike timing can be represented by the stated rate-change rule.
neurips-1999-spike-based-learning-rules-.tldr: Under certain conditions, anti-Hebbian spike-timing plasticity becomes a firing-rate-change rule that stabilizes persistent network activity.

paragraphs: The paper studies how hierarchical reinforcement learning can ignore selected aspects of the state while still learning reliably. It distinguishes state abstraction from temporal abstraction, where a higher-level action may execute many primitive actions before ending. State abstraction instead simplifies what the learner represents about its situation.

The authors work within MAXQ, a framework that decomposes the value function for a hierarchy of tasks. They define five conditions under which state abstraction can be combined with this decomposition. These conditions provide a formal basis for deciding when aspects of the state can be omitted while preserving the stated learning guarantee.

They prove that MAXQ-Q learning converges under those conditions and present experiments showing that state abstraction is important for successful application of the algorithm. The theoretical result is conditional on the specified requirements. Together, the proof and experiments connect representational simplification with both convergence and practical learning, explaining how a hierarchy can benefit from simplifying the states used within it.
neurips-1999-state-abstraction-in-maxq-h.tldr: Five conditions allow state abstraction in MAXQ with a convergence proof, while experiments show its practical importance.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of applying familiar machine-learning algorithms to datasets containing many examples and very many dimensions. The authors introduce the Parallel Problems Server and MATLAB*P, which together let users work on large datasets from within Matlab using networked computers. The goal is to make scientific-computing resources accessible through a familiar interactive environment.

The systems are designed to make this larger-scale computation transparent to the user. This matters for researchers who already have working Matlab implementations: access to additional computational power is more useful when existing algorithm code can remain largely recognizable. The contribution concerns the computational environment supporting machine learning as well as the applications it enables.

The authors demonstrate several tasks, including independent component analysis on text corpora containing tens of thousands of documents. That example requires only minimal changes to the original Matlab implementation. It illustrates how the system can extend the reach of existing methods and make previously inaccessible data available for examining both the datasets and the behavior of the algorithms.
neurips-1999-the-parallel-problems-serve.tldr: PPServer and MATLAB*P enable large-scale machine learning from Matlab, including text analysis with minimal changes to existing code.

paragraphs: The paper investigates when a support vector machine has a unique solution. It covers both pattern recognition and regression estimation for a general class of cost functions. The authors give necessary and sufficient conditions, providing a characterization of uniqueness rather than only a condition that guarantees it in some cases.

They show that non-uniqueness requires all support vectors to be at their bounds and give examples of non-unique solutions. The direction of this statement matters: having every support vector at a bound does not by itself establish non-uniqueness. They also explain that uniqueness in the primal optimization problem need not imply uniqueness in the dual, or vice versa.

A further contribution concerns the threshold parameter b. When all support vectors are at their bounds, the usual method for determining this threshold fails. The authors show how to compute it when the solution is nevertheless unique. This addresses a concrete consequence of the uniqueness analysis, distinguishing an exceptional computational case from the existence of multiple solutions.
neurips-1999-uniqueness-of-the-svm-solut.tldr: The paper characterizes SVM solution uniqueness and explains how to compute the threshold in a unique all-at-bound case.
